source_text: Voluntas ergo, quae nihil est aliud quam motus animi cogente nullo, possibilitatem suam naturae debet, effectum suum sibi. In natura enim exorta est, sed a possibili, non a necessario. Hic si dicat aliquis: Sed mala natura, quae potuit habere voluntatem malam; respondeo: Sed bona natura, quae potuit habere voluntatem bonam. Uno ergo tempore optima simul pessimaque dicetur. At id rerum ratio non sinit, ut uno eodemque tempore una eademque res contrariis meritorum qualitatibus impleatur. Si igitur ideo mala putetur, quia potuit malum facere; ideo bona credatur, quia potuit bonum operari. Cur autem, inquit, et malum potuit, quae bonum operabatur? Respondeo: Quia bonum hoc, quod virtus dicitur, proprium esse non poterat, nisi fuisset voluntarium; voluntarium autem non esset, si necessitatem boni habuisset; necessitatem autem boni pertulisset, si non habuisset possibilitatem mali. Ut ergo constaret ius boni, admissa est possibilitas mali.
pass_a_gloss: Will therefore, which is nothing other than a motion of the mind no one compelling, owes its possibility to nature, its effect to itself. For it arose in nature, but from the possible, not from the necessary. Here if someone says: But an evil nature, which could have an evil will; I reply: But a good nature, which could have a good will. At one time therefore it will be called best and worst together. But the reason of things does not allow that, that at one and the same time one and the same thing be filled with contrary qualities of deserts. If therefore it is thought evil because it could do evil; let it be believed good because it could work good. But why, he says, could it also evil, which was working good? I reply: Because this good, which is called virtue, could not be its own, unless it had been voluntary; but it would not be voluntary, if it had had a necessity of good; but it would have borne a necessity of good, if it had not had a possibility of evil. That therefore the right of good might stand, a possibility of evil was admitted.

pass_b_english: Will, then, which is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, owes its possibility to nature and its result to itself. It arose within nature, but from possibility, not necessity. If someone says here, ‘But a nature capable of an evil will is evil,’ I answer, ‘But a nature capable of a good will is good.’ It would therefore be called excellent and utterly evil at the same time. Yet the nature of things does not permit one and the same thing at one and the same time to be filled with opposing moral qualities. If it is thought evil because it could do evil, let it be believed good because it could do good. ‘Why,’ he asks, ‘could the nature that did good also do evil?’ I answer: because this good called virtue could not belong to the person as his own unless it were voluntary. It would not be voluntary if it carried the necessity of good; it would have suffered the necessity of good if it had not possessed the possibility of evil. Therefore, to preserve the right of good, the possibility of evil was admitted.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian contrasts opportunity/help with imposed necessity; load-bearing against natural compulsion to sin.
